title: Clothes remember
hook: Hasidic dress keeps the memory of old Eastern Europe

segments.voice: Yesterday, the courts: Ger, Belz, Satmar, Bobov, each one named for towns its Hasidim may never have seen. Did you say the name of a place you carry? Day one thousand two hundred four.

A closet holds a story if you know how to read it. A wedding dress in a garment bag. A grandfather's watch in a drawer. A sports jersey that only comes out on game day. On a Friday afternoon in a Hasidic neighborhood, the men come out in long black silk coats, and some wear round fur hats, wide and tall, that look like nothing else on the street. To a passerby it looks like a costume. To the people wearing it, it's closer to that watch in the drawer. Today's word is what the cloth is holding.
screen: `A CLOSET HOLDS A STORY.` → `FRIDAY AFTERNOON.` → `NOT A COSTUME.`

segments.voice: Clothes remember. Turn it four ways. First, the pieces. The long coat, called a bekishe or a kapote. The fur hat on Shabbat, a shtreimel, or in some courts a taller one, a spodik. A belt, the gartel, tied around the waist for prayer. Each court has its own details, down to the way a hat is shaped. Second, the memory. Tradition says this is, broadly, how Jewish men and nobles in parts of Eastern Europe once dressed. The world around them changed its clothes. The Hasidim kept theirs. So the coat becomes a way of saying: we have not forgotten where we come from. A midrash some Hasidim quote says that in Egypt the Israelites held on to their own names and their own language, and some versions add their own dress. Third, dressing for God. The Talmud tells of a sage who would put on fine shoes before praying, citing the prophet Amos: "prepare to meet thy God, O Israel." Hasidim speak of the gartel in the same spirit, a line drawn around the body before standing to pray. Fourth, what it isn't. The clothes are not the faith, and Hasidim themselves don't say they are. Other Jews dress in all kinds of ways and pray just as seriously. But cloth can hold a memory the way a melody can. Now look back over this week. Two souls. Always joyful. You can repair. Truth, fiercely. Hidden will. Named for towns. And today, a coat that remembers.
screen: `BEKISHE, SHTREIMEL, GARTEL.` · `THE WORLD CHANGED; THEY DIDN'T.` · `PREPARE TO MEET THY GOD.` · `CLOTH HOLDS A MEMORY.` · then, large: `CLOTHES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dress with meaning once. Sit, and breathe. Look down at what you're wearing right now. Pick one thing: a ring, a scarf, a shirt, a pair of shoes. Ask where it came from. Who gave it, where you bought it, what you were doing the first time you wore it. Let the memory come up. Then choose one item you'll put on deliberately tomorrow, for a reason you can name: to honor someone, to mark a day, to get ready for something that matters. The bell holds the time.
Clothes remember. Hasidic dress, the long coat, the fur hat, the prayer belt, keeps the memory of old Eastern Europe and turns getting dressed into getting ready. Today's word.
Your line: clothes remember. Today, as you get dressed or undressed, touch one thing you're wearing and recall where it came from. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: In Hasidic courts, men wear a long dark coat and tie a gartel for prayer, and on Shabbat and festivals married men in some courts put on a fur shtreimel or spodik; the details differ from court to court.

notes: Shabbat 10a: Rava bar Rav Huna putting on fine shoes (or socks) before prayer, citing Amos 4:12; please confirm the attribution.

Midrash on Israel in Egypt keeping names and language: the classic versions (Leviticus Rabbah 32:5; Mekhilta) list names and language; the addition of dress appears in some later citations. Stated as 'some versions add'; please confirm.
The gartel's meaning (separating upper and lower body for prayer, related to Shulchan Aruch OC 91:2) is described only loosely as 'a line drawn around the body'.
Origins of Hasidic dress stated broadly ('how Jewish men and nobles in parts of Eastern Europe once dressed'); please confirm or soften.
Week look-back (days 1198–1204) placed at the end of the teach.
Editor: the origin of Hasidic dress is now framed as 'tradition says'; the look-back's 'two souls in each person' shortened to 'two souls', since the Tanya speaks of each Jew.
